chapter_theme: The kaathai of the evening: in one long sentence the poet brings dusk on Puhar like a usurping king, lets the Pandya crescent take the sky, and goes through the city's nights, Madhavi giving Kovalan love and its quarrels, the wives asleep on their husbands' chests, Kannaki stripped of every ornament but the marriage one, the parted women sleepless and weeping, until at dawn the god of desire, who patrolled all night, is declared the city's best watchman; a venba sets the moon as a king's umbrella, shade to Madhavi and heat to Kannaki.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, left alone in his house
Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer with whom Kovalan now lives
the wives of Puhar who sleep on their husbands' chests through the night
the women of Puhar parted from their lovers
Kama, the god of desire, with the makara banner, flower arrows and sugarcane bow

silappathikaram:4:1-20.reading: The poet brings evening on Puhar as a political disaster: the sun, sole wheel-ruler of the world, is gone, the earth like a woman in grief weeps with pale face and wet eyes as if her king were lost, and evening camps in the city like a foreign king who seizes a land whose victorious king is absent, sides with the traitors and leaves the loyal wringing their hands; lovers apart are grieved and lovers together delighted, a bee hums in the jasmine beside the herdsmen, the little breeze scatters scent through the streets and women light the gem lamps.
silappathikaram:4:1-20.nuance: The whole kaathai is one sentence, and this opening sets its frame: evening as a usurper in a kingless land (lines 8 to 12), a figure drawn from the state rather than from love. Lines 13 and 14 announce the chapter's plan, the same hour bringing grief to the parted and joy to the joined, which the following units fill in house by house. The herdsmen of line 15 are கோவலர், the hero's name in the plural; the chapter does not stress the pun, and I note it only as a sound a listener would hear.
silappathikaram:4:1-20.event: Evening falls on Puhar and the women of the houses light the gem lamps.
silappathikaram:4:1-20.unit_note: Boundary moved from 21|22 to 20|21: line 20 (மாலைவந்து இருத்தென) closes the clause of evening's arrival, and lines 21 to 22 (இளையர் ஆயினும் ... குலமுதல் ஆகலின்) give the reason for the crescent's power in the next clause.

silappathikaram:4:21-34.reading: Because it is the founder of the line of the Pandyas, who drive off hostile kings even when young, the white crescent rises in the evening sky, routs the raiding gloom, spreads milk-white rays without swerving from its nature and rules the stars; under its light Madhavi, adorned, on the high moonlit terrace among beds of jasmine and mallikai, gives Kovalan both love-making and the feigned quarrel, meeting him with an eager heart.
silappathikaram:4:21-34.nuance: The moon that took over the sky from the beaten evening is a Pandya; in a book whose second half turns on a Pandya's justice, its first praise of that line is of a ruler that does not swerve (பான்மையில் திரியாது). Madhavi is given both கலவி and புலவி, union and the lovers' sulk, as a skill she offers Kovalan (அளித்து), an art and not only a feeling. The unit ends on அன்றியும் ('and besides'): she is the first item in a list of the city's nights.
silappathikaram:4:21-34.event: Madhavi, adorned on her moonlit terrace, receives Kovalan with love-making and lovers' quarrels.
silappathikaram:4:21-34.unit_note: Start moved from 22 to 21 to take in the whole reason clause (lines 21 to 22) that belongs to the crescent of line 23; the unit still ends at 34 (மாதவி அன்றியும்).

silappathikaram:4:35-46.reading: Besides Madhavi, the other wives of the city lie on rich flower beds strewn with western white incense, eastern dark agil, northern stone-ground and southern sandal, lotus, lily and garlands mixed with fine powder, and, drowsy in the gentle south wind, sleep in delight folded on their husbands' chests.
silappathikaram:4:35-46.nuance: The four directions of the perfumes (குடதிசை, குணதிசை, வடமலை, தென்மலை) make the bed a map of the merchant city's trade, so the joy of these couples is also a picture of Puhar's wealth. Their wedded sleep (கொழுநர் அகலத்து ஒடுங்கி) is the one thing Kannaki, also a wife, lacks in the next unit.
silappathikaram:4:35-46.event: The wives of Puhar sleep in delight on their husbands' chests.
silappathikaram:4:35-46.unit_note: End moved from 44 to 46: the sentence of the scented beds runs on through lines 45 and 46 and closes at களித்துயில் எய்த; Kannaki's description begins at line 47.

silappathikaram:4:47-57.reading: Kannaki, with a helpless heart, has left off the anklets from her feet and the girdle from her waist, draws no saffron on her breast, takes pleasure in no ornament but the auspicious one, has put away her earrings, forgets the collyrium of her eyes, loses the tilaka from her brow and the oil from her hair, and her bright smile is lost to Kovalan.
silappathikaram:4:47-57.nuance: Each line strips one ornament, and the verbs are of absence and forgetting (ஒழிய, நீங்க, மறப்ப, இழப்ப), not of protest: she makes no speech in the chapter. Only one loss is charged to another, the smile Kovalan forfeits (தவள வாள்நகை கோவலன் இழப்ப, line 55). Line 50 (மங்கல அணியின் பிறிதுஅணி மகிழாள்) answers Kovalan's own praise at the wedding night (silappathikaram:2:51-66), and the first anklet of the epic appears here, laid aside.
silappathikaram:4:47-57.event: Kannaki, alone at evening, puts off her anklets and every ornament but the auspicious marriage ornament.
silappathikaram:4:47-57.unit_note: Both boundaries moved: the unit now starts at 47 (அணிசிலம்பு ஒழிய, the first item of Kannaki's description) and ends at 57, where கண்ணகி அன்றியும் closes it; the original 45-62 split her description from its subject's name and ran into the parted women.

silappathikaram:4:58-71.reading: The women parted from their lovers sigh like the bellows of a smith's furnace and shrink into themselves; they leave the summer bedroom, close the small windows of the cool-season room, keep sandal and pearl strings off their breasts, shun beds strewn with lily and red waterlily and find no sleep on pillows stuffed with the down of mated swans; and in their sulking with their husbands their long eyes, red at the corners, rain pearls of lonely tears.
silappathikaram:4:58-71.nuance: Lines 58 and 59 repeat almost word for word the Akananuru's evening of a woman left behind (akananuru:71: காதலர்ப் பிரிந்த புலம்பின் நோதக, and the breath blown in a furnace), so a single heroine's lament becomes one class of the city's women. The swan-down pillow is of 'mated swans' (துணைபுணர் அன்னம்), a comfort made from the union they lack. Lines 68 to 71 shift to the time of ஊடல் with husbands, and I cannot fix whether these are the same parted women remembering past quarrels or another group of wives in a quarrel now.
silappathikaram:4:58-71.event: The women parted from their lovers lie sleepless, refusing the comforts of their rooms.
silappathikaram:4:58-71.unit_note: The original unit 63-84 is split, and its start moved to 58: the parted women's sentence begins at காதலர்ப் பிரிந்த மாதர் (line 58) and its tears close at உறைப்ப (line 71); the dawn scene opens at line 72.

silappathikaram:4:72-84.reading: Until dawn comes and night departs, when the pond, a woman with a swan's gait, lily breath, lotus mouth and hair of sand, wakes to bees singing a mournful mode and opens her blue-lily eyes, and drums and conches sound in turn and rouse the sea-girt town, Kama of the makara banner, carrying his flower arrows and sugarcane bow, roamed sleepless at midnight and by day, and so the city's watch was kept supremely well.
silappathikaram:4:72-84.nuance: The closing word is a joke on the chapter's political opening: the city that evening invaded like a usurper is guarded all night, and its guard is the god of desire, whose 'patrol' is what kept the parted women awake. நோதிறம், the mode the bees sing at dawn, is a pann of grief, so even the waking of the pond carries the night's sorrow.
silappathikaram:4:72-84.event: Kama roams Puhar through the night until drums and conches wake the town at dawn.
silappathikaram:4:72-84.unit_note: Split from the original 63-84: the dawn clause starts at அன்னம் மெல்நடை (line 72) after the parted women's tears close at உறைப்ப (line 71); the unit ends where the kaathai does (line 84).

silappathikaram:4:85-88.reading: The closing venba says that the night, when the moon riding the sky spread its light and opened the buds, showed itself to Madhavi who was with her lover and to Kannaki like the guardian king's white umbrella, which is shade to those joined to him and heat to those who are not.
silappathikaram:4:85-88.nuance: கூடினார், 'those joined', serves both halves of the simile: allies of the king and lovers together. Madhavi is called கூடிய and Kannaki is given no epithet, so the poem's sorting of the two women is done by one word and by its absence.

claims.claim: a guardian king's umbrella is cool shade to those joined to him and burns those who are not

links.note: At the wedding night Kovalan asks why her admirers decked her with other ornaments besides the flawless auspicious one (மறுஇல் மங்கல அணியே அன்றியும் பிறிதுஅணி); alone at evening she delights in no ornament but the auspicious one (மங்கல அணியின் பிறிதுஅணி மகிழாள்).
links.teaches: The husband's compliment that she needs no ornament but the marriage one comes true literally as the mark of his desertion, so the poet builds her abandonment out of his own flattery.

links.note: The anklets Kannaki leaves off in grief (அணிசிலம்பு ஒழிய) are the anklets she offers with a smile when Kovalan returns ruined and sees her wasted body (சிலம்புஉள கொண்மின்).
links.teaches: The epic's fatal anklet enters the story as an ornament set aside in loneliness, and that unworn state is what lets it become the capital for the journey to Madurai.

links.note: The crescent is praised as founder of the Pandya line and as ruling the stars without swerving from its nature (பான்மையில் திரியாது); in kaathai 20 a Pandya, umbrella drooping and sceptre slack, calls himself the thief.
links.teaches: The epic's first word on the Pandya line is a praise of unswerving rule set over a scene of Kovalan's straying, and the later verdict turns that praise against its own king; the tension rests on reading the moon's constancy as the line's.

links.note: The benediction hails the moon because it is like the Chola's cool white umbrella sheltering the world; the venba makes the moon like a guardian king's white umbrella that is shade to the joined and heat to the rest.
links.teaches: The umbrella that the opening praised as sheltering everyone is here given its second edge, and the edge falls on Kannaki: royal protection, like love, covers only those inside the bond.

links.note: Both have women parted from their lovers at evening (காதலر்ப் பிரிந்த, nearly the same half-line), and both liken their breath to air blown in a smith's furnace.
links.teaches: The epic takes a Sangam paalai heroine's evening lament nearly verbatim and turns it from one woman's crisis into a class of Puhar's women, one entry in a survey of the city's nights.

gains.a: the epic's brief list gains the depth of a full lament, the friend, the fear of death in the evening, that its two lines only gesture at
gains.b: the Akananuru poem gains evidence that its furnace image and half-line had become stock diction a later poet could cite as a type

links.note: The Kural's woman hears the herdsman's flute as evening's envoy and a killing weapon; the epic sets the herdsmen's music and the humming bee over an evening that grieves the parted and delights the joined.
links.teaches: Heard together, the two show that the flute's cruelty lies in the listener's separation, not in the sound, since the same pastoral music opens a night of delight for others in the epic.

gains.a: the epic's impartial evening gains the inside of one parted listener, for whom its music is a weapon
gains.b: the couplet gains a wider scene in which its deadly flute is, for other hearers, simply the sign of nightfall

links.note: The Kural's woman says the whole town reels in sorrow when evening spreads; the venba says the same moonlit night is cool to Madhavi with her lover and hot to Kannaki without him.
links.teaches: The parted woman's sense that the whole town suffers with her is set against a city where one night divides two women of the same house's story, which shows her claim is the projection of grief.

gains.a: the venba's neat sorting of two women gains the parted woman's own conviction that evening is a public calamity
gains.b: the couplet's town-wide sorrow is shown to be a single woman's view, since the epic's city is split by the same hour

source_issues: The kaathai has 88 lines in the core text but the edition's printed numbering ends at 80, so line numbers here (the kaathai's own, 1-88 as `show` prints them) differ from the printed ones.
Line 66 (துணைபுணர் அன்னத் தூவியிற் செறித்த) carries a repaired encoding flag (a TSCII leftover read as ூ); the repaired reading makes sense and I marked it as written.
